No, that's not right, and it matters for your design.

A language model on its own remembers nothing between conversations. Each request is a fresh start. The model sees only the text you send it in that one request, and then it writes a reply. Nothing is stored inside it. That's why a chatbot seems to remember earlier turns in a chat: the app re-sends the whole conversation each time. It's tempting to think the model remembers, because the app makes it look that way.

Here is an example for your makerspace assistant. Last week, Dana told it, "I finished the laser cutter safety training." This week, Dana asks, "Can I book the laser cutter?" If you send only that question, the model has no idea who Dana is or what she did. If your code saved Dana's training status in a file or database last week, looked it up, and put "Dana completed laser cutter training" into this week's request, the model can use it. So memory is something you build around the model.

This ties directly to your mission goal of deciding what the assistant saves between sessions. Two things follow:
- You choose what to save (training status, probably not every chat message).
- You choose what to put back into each request. Everything you add costs tokens, so it also affects your budget.

We haven't covered context windows or memory patterns yet. I can write a lesson on them if you'd like, since it's the next step in your plan.

Quick check: if Dana's status is saved in your database but your code never adds it to the request, what does the model know about her?
